terms.def: A type of law that organizes how land is used across the city. At its core, zoning specifies the range of allowed uses for a property and governs the size and shape of its buildings.

One of the "zones" the city's land is divided into, each with its own set of land use regulations. Every NYC district name begins with R (Residence), C (Commercial) or M (Manufacturing), followed by a number showing density or intensity, such as R6B, C2-4 or M1-2.

Zoning districts for housing and community facilities like schools and hospitals. There are twelve levels of increasing density: R1 through R5 are often considered lower-density, R6 through R8 medium-density, and R9 through R12 high-density.

Zoning districts that allow a range of commercial and community facility uses, and in most cases housing. They range in intensity (scale and type of commercial activity) from C1 to C8. C1 and C2 are neighborhood retail districts; C4 through C6 are the principal shopping and business districts; the others fill more specialized roles.
Zoning districts that allow manufacturing and commercial uses, and in some cases community facilities. They range from M1 (light) to M2 (medium) to M3 (heavy) manufacturing.

A letter or number appended to a zoning district name (for example the "-2" in M1-2 or the "A" in R3A). Suffixes generally reflect subtle variations in permitted building scale; an M1-2 district typically allows one or two more stories than an M1-1. A rule listing "R3" applies to all R3 variations, while one listing only "R3-2" applies just to that variation.

Rules setting out where different kinds of activities may be located in the city. They sort out which uses belong together in each district so that activities that do not mix well, such as polluting factories and homes, are not permitted in the same district.

Rules that establish the size and shape of buildings and how a building is positioned on a property, so buildings fit their neighborhood and light and air reach the street, neighbors and occupants. Floor area, yards, lot coverage, and height and setback rules are all bulk regulations.

Rules that manage the flow of people and goods by setting how much off-street parking is required or allowed. More vehicle-dependent areas may have a minimum number of required spaces; transit-rich areas often have no minimum and may have a maximum instead.

The law that contains New York City's zoning regulations. It has a map portion showing where every zoning district applies and a text portion containing all the rules, organized into 14 Articles plus Appendices. The current Resolution took effect on December 15, 1961.

The map portion of the Zoning Resolution: 126 individual maps on a grid of 35 numbered sections, most divided into "a" through "d" sub-maps (for example 8D or 13B). The official "paper" maps (in pdf form) control; ZoLa is not the official zoning map. Each map notes its most recent rezoning and ULURP number.

The text portion of the Zoning Resolution containing all the rules, organized into 14 Articles (numbered with Roman numerals), each divided into up to nine chapters, then sections. Articles II, III and IV set baseline rules for Residence, Commercial and Manufacturing Districts. There is no printed version; DCP stopped printing it in 2017.

The baseline rules of a zoning district found in Articles II, III and IV. They are called "underlying" because they may be, and often are, modified or superseded by Special Purpose Districts or rules for geographically specific areas.

An area where the underlying zoning rules are modified to fit local goals. Each has its own chapter in Articles VIII to XIV and a one- to three-letter designation (for example "OP" for the Special Ocean Parkway District). They appear as gray tone on the zoning map; darker gray marks where two overlap. The handbook says there are currently 59.

A building that adheres to all applicable zoning rules and can receive a building permit without any special permission from a planning agency. Most new buildings in New York are constructed as-of-right.

An approval that modifies zoning rules, such as a zoning map or text amendment, authorization, special permit or variance. Each involves public review, including environmental review, and decision-makers (the CPC or BSA) have discretion to request revisions or say yes or no.
Relief from zoning rules granted when a property has irregularities and the rules create an unusual hardship. Variances act as a relief valve so zoning is not too onerous in outlier cases.

A change to the zoning map, often called a rezoning, used when the mapped district does not allow the desired uses or building scale. Zoning map amendments follow ULURP, including Community Board, Borough President, City Planning Commission and City Council review.

A change to the rules in the zoning text. Like map changes, applicants prepare a land use application with DCP, and the change goes through public review and votes before taking effect. Dozens of map and text amendments are adopted each year.

The application, prepared with the Department of City Planning, to change zoning or obtain another land use approval. It includes any required environmental review. Once DCP certifies it as complete, it goes before the City Planning Commission and public review begins.
The legal document that establishes the organization, powers, functions and procedures of City government, including the sequence of public review for zoning changes.

The structured public review process, with a set timeline for each phase, that zoning map amendments and CPC special permits follow. It includes input from the affected Community Board and Borough President, a CPC public hearing and vote and, if approved by the CPC, a City Council vote. It is the most stringent of the review procedures.
The commission that holds public hearings and votes on zoning changes and grants special permits, authorizations and certifications under the Zoning Resolution.
The City agency that applicants work with to prepare land use applications, that publishes the Zoning Handbook and Online ZR, and that runs the Zoning Help Desk (212-720-3291).

A document issued by the Department of Buildings when a building is finished, verifying that it is safe to be occupied. For affordable housing under MIH or UAP, HPD must sign off on the finished units before DOB can issue the CO.

The Department of Buildings checks plans for compliance with the Construction Codes and the Zoning Resolution before issuing a building permit, and is responsible for ongoing enforcement of zoning, including inspecting and issuing zoning violations.
Zoning districts developed from the 1980s onward and mapped broadly across the city to preserve existing neighborhood character, prevent out-of-scale development and encourage right-sized growth.

A set of 2023 to 2024 citywide zoning reforms: City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality (energy-efficient buildings and alternative energy infrastructure), City of Yes for Economic Opportunity (modernized use rules allowing a wider range of compatible uses), and City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (more housing types in low-density areas and broader affordable housing programs). DCP calls it the largest change since 1961.

One of ten categories into which zoning organizes all uses: I Agriculture/Open; II Residences; III Community Facilities; IV Public Service/Administrative; V Transient; VI Retail and Services; VII Offices and Laboratories; VIII Recreation; IX Storage; X Production. Four groups have lettered subcategories, and over 250 individual uses are listed in use group tables.

A limit on the size of a use, by square footage or number of seats, so it fits its district. For example, clothing and department stores cannot exceed 10,000 square feet in neighborhood commercial districts. Limits apply to individual businesses, not the total of the use on a lot. Marked "S" in use group tables.

In Commercial and Manufacturing Districts uses generally must be in enclosed buildings, but zoning lets certain uses, or low-impact parts of them, occur outdoors, such as agriculture, outdoor skating rinks, restaurant outdoor dining and, in Manufacturing Districts, outdoor storage. Marked "U" in use group tables.

Limits on noise, air pollution and other nuisances that apply to a range of uses in Manufacturing Districts, such as food manufacturing and auto repair. More restrictive standards apply in light manufacturing districts than heavier ones.

Conditions placed on specific uses so they do not harm their surroundings, such as performance standards, limits on housing units or building types in some low-density districts, or required indoor waiting space for theaters in high-density commercial areas. Marked "P" in use group tables.

Rules on where uses may go within a building. In neighborhood commercial districts, commercial uses are limited to the lower two stories, with extra restrictions where commercial and residential uses share the second story. In central business districts commercial uses may be on any story, with limited allowances above residences.

A use that is incidental to and customarily found with the primary use, on the same property, for the benefit of its users, such as a pizza shop's storage room. If it grows to overwhelm the primary use (for example renting storage to others) it is treated as a separate primary use.

A small business run from a house or apartment, allowed as an accessory use as-of-right in all residences. Significantly updated in 2024, the defined term sets size and operational controls, including environmental regulations and a prohibition on business signs. See ZR Section 12-10.

A citywide framework adopted in 2024 for the ground floors of buildings in Commercial Districts, replacing a patchwork of earlier rules. It has three levels, Tiers A, B and C, with stricter design standards at each tier.

The lightest streetscape rules, for commercial streets far from transit: limits on blank walls and where parking spaces can go on the lot. Areas near highway ramps and large shopping complexes are exempt.

Streetscape rules for major commercial corridors near transit. They restrict ground floor apartments and infrastructure uses, limit residential lobbies (under 50 feet wide), amenities, parking and loading, and require part of the ground floor to have windows (transparency).

The strictest streetscape rules, applied on specified streets (for example in some Special Purpose Districts and many Manhattan avenues). They require commercial use continuity, limit residential lobbies to under 25 feet wide, and bar parking lots, curb cuts and loading docks.
A sign that promotes a business, product or service on the same zoning lot, such as a sign above a pizza shop.

A sign that promotes a business, product or service located off the zoning lot, such as a billboard. Allowed in Manufacturing Districts but may not light up or flash there; generally restricted in Residence Districts.

Zoning rules on sign type, size, illumination and location. Residence Districts allow mainly small unlit nameplates and identification signs. In C1 and C2 districts a sign may equal three times the street frontage, up to a maximum of 150 square feet, with each storefront calculating from its own frontage.

A use that predates and does not conform with today's use rules, such as older housing in a Manufacturing District or a small store in a Residence District. It may remain indefinitely. If the space stays vacant more than two years, only conforming uses may re-occupy it, though small older shops in Residence Districts are exempt from that time limit.

The floor space in a building that counts toward zoning limits. Some spaces are exempt, such as cellars, mechanical rooms, elevator bulkheads, trash rooms, and space for parking and loading, so gross building area is often 10 to 20 percent larger than zoning floor area.

Zoning's primary bulk tool: the maximum floor area allowed divided by lot area. Multiply lot size by the FAR to get total buildable floor area (a 10,000 square foot lot at 1.0 FAR allows 10,000 square feet). District FARs range from 0.5 to 18.0, higher in some Special Purpose Districts. Pronounced "F-A-R."

Districts often set different maximum FARs for residential, commercial and community facility uses. These are not added together: the highest maximum FAR among uses on the lot sets the overall limit, and each use must stay within its own maximum.
Building space fully or predominantly below grade. Cellars are exempt from zoning floor area.
Rules that define where a building can be placed on a site, such as yards and lot coverage. They differ based on whether the zoning lot is a corner, through or interior lot.
Any lot within one hundred feet of the point of intersection of two or more streets. Corner lots have no rear yard requirement and are allowed higher lot coverage.
Any lot that touches two parallel streets and is not a corner lot. Through lots have no rear lot line and instead must provide "rear yard equivalents."
Any zoning lot that is neither a corner lot nor a through lot.

An open area along a property line where a building cannot be constructed, except for permitted obstructions. There are front, side and rear yards. Front and side yards are mostly required in low-density Residence Districts; rear yards apply in all districts, typically 20 feet deep, reflecting the city's "doughnut" block pattern.
Open area required on through lots, which have no rear lot line, to match the rear yards of more typical lots. It can often be placed elsewhere on the lot.

The percentage of a lot that buildings may cover, typically applying in Residence Districts and to residential buildings elsewhere. Allowances range from 40 to 100 percent, increasing with density and higher on corner lots.

A building element zoning allows inside required yards or coverage areas, or beyond the height and setback envelope, such as porches, chimneys, balconies, bay windows, solar panels, parapets, dormers and accessory dwelling units. They often have size and height limits.

Created in 2024, a small additional housing unit allowed on a lot with a one- or two-family home, such as a backyard cottage, garage conversion or basement apartment. Restrictions apply in some areas over flooding and neighborhood context. An ADU can be a permitted obstruction in a rear yard, and no parking is required for it. See ZR Section 12-10.

Rules that shape the volume of a building above its footprint, defining the "envelope" its permitted floor area must fit within, so new buildings do not overwhelm their surroundings while still allowing design flexibility.

The envelope required for single- and two-family houses in lowest-density districts that require side yards. The perimeter wall may be up to 25 feet; above that the building must slope inward and never exceed 35 feet.

The envelope for districts that allow rowhouses and apartment buildings with flat roofs. Maximum heights range from 35 to hundreds of feet depending on district. Districts with letter suffixes typically require all buildings to follow flat roof envelopes.

The height of the lower part of a building closest to the street (its "base"). Zoning sets a maximum base height so new buildings do not overwhelm the street, and may set a minimum to provide a sense of enclosure.
The minimum distance a building must step back from the street above its base height. Deeper setbacks are required on narrow streets. After the setback the building can rise to its maximum height.

An imaginary, diagonally sloping plane that begins at a set height above the street line and slopes upward and inward; buildings must sit behind it so light and air reach the street. Starting height and angle increase with density. It often applies to non-residential buildings in districts without letter suffixes.

In the highest-density districts, a building portion allowed to rise above the sky exposure plane or base height with no absolute height limit, in exchange for setting back from streets and limiting tower lot coverage (typically 40 to 65 percent).

A building's facade facing the street. Street wall rules often require a share of the wall to sit near the sidewalk (for example within 8 feet for 70 percent of its length). In "B" suffix districts, new buildings must line up with neighboring townhouses.
Allowances for portions of a required street wall to project forward or recess backward, such as bay windows on townhouses, giving designers flexibility and echoing older buildings.

Minimum lot area and lot width rules governing how a larger lot can be divided, most impactful for single- and two-family houses in lower-density areas. The largest minimums apply in the lowest-density districts.

The number used to cap the number of apartments on a zoning lot. In most areas, the maximum is permitted residential floor area divided by 680 square feet (20,000 square feet allows 29 units). It sets a minimum average unit size, not a minimum size per unit. Some housing, such as in the Manhattan Core and Downtown Brooklyn, is exempt.

Space, indoors or outdoors and accessible to all residents, that new apartment buildings with nine or more units must provide, equal to three percent of residential floor area (for example a rooftop patio or basement gym).
Required separation, ranging from 10 to 80 feet, when a single lot includes more than one building and one contains residences. The required distance increases with density and building height.

An open area, such as an older building's courtyard, that apartment windows may face to receive light and air. Courts must meet minimum dimensions; they are often used at the rear of corner-lot buildings, which have no rear yard.

Extra floor area granted in exchange for providing a public amenity, such as a public plaza, visual or performing arts space, subway improvements, theater preservation or a grocery store. Some bonuses are as-of-right; others need CPC and City Council approval.

A public plaza provided on private property in exchange for a floor area bonus; the oldest zoning bonus. A plaza bonus requires CPC Chair certification that it meets detailed design rules (ZR Section 37-70).
Moving unused floor area from one site to another to further planning goals, for example from a landmark to nearby zoning lots, or from required open areas in specified cases.

Combining two or more adjacent zoning lots into one larger lot, so buildable floor area can shift around the merged lot as-of-right. The merged lot must follow all bulk rules. Mergers often preserve older buildings by moving their unused floor area next door.

A building that predates and violates one or more current bulk rules, such as height or FAR. It may remain indefinitely and be changed if no new non-compliance is created or worsened, with special allowances for resiliency, accessibility, energy retrofits and residential conversions. If damaged or demolished, it can be rebuilt if at least 25 percent remains standing.
Rules setting how much parking a new development must provide, based on its location and proposed uses. Housing is calculated by number of dwelling units; retail by store square footage.

terms.term: Manhattan Core and Long Island City (parking areas)
terms.def: Areas where zoning requires no parking for any use. The Manhattan Core is Community Districts 1 to 8; it has strict limits on permitted parking and does not allow off-site parking. Their parking rules are in Article I, Chapters 3 and 6.
A parking area where zoning does not require parking for residential developments and often not for non-residential developments.
A parking area where zoning requires parking only for large residential developments and some non-residential developments. It is part of the Greater Transit Zone.

The combined transit-oriented parking area that the handbook's charts divide into the Inner Transit Zone and Outer Transit Zone. Outside it ("beyond the Greater Transit Zone"), parking is required for most residential and non-residential developments.
Groupings of similar non-residential uses used to calculate how much parking each requires.
A provision that removes calculated parking requirements for small lots or where the number of required spaces is small. Waivers vary by zoning district, parking area and use.

All non-required accessory parking a site may voluntarily provide, subject to maximums. South of Central Park, spaces are limited to 20 percent of dwelling units and never more than 200; elsewhere up to two spaces per dwelling unit in a multiple dwelling, and never more than 200.

Required parking located on a separate lot within specified distances and districts, such as a Residence District site using parking in a Commercial District a block or two away. Not allowed in the Manhattan Core.
Rules on the size, number and location of curb cuts accessing parking and loading, ensuring access while limiting effects on sidewalks and on-street parking.

An off-street space where trucks pick up or deliver goods, required for new buildings with commercial or manufacturing uses. The number depends on use, size and district; uses are grouped into five Loading Requirement Categories. Loading areas are exempt from floor area up to 150 percent of the required amount.

New multi-family residential, community facility and commercial developments must provide secure bicycle parking. Multi-family buildings need one enclosed space per two dwelling units. Bicycle parking areas are exempt from floor area, within limits.

Most developments at the water's edge must provide public open space along it, with design and operational standards. Small lots, low-density residences and heavy manufacturing uses are exempt. Rules are in Article VI, Chapter 2.
A requirement along certain streets that new buildings set back and extend the sidewalk onto their property by a defined number of feet to handle pedestrian traffic.

Space on a development site next to a train station that the transit agency may request for station improvements, such as an elevator. Floor space in a transit easement volume is exempt from floor area and extra height may be allowed. Rules are in Article VI, Chapter 6.

Most new buildings must provide street trees along the sidewalk; in low-density Residence Districts a planting strip along the curb is also required. The Department of Parks and Recreation can exempt sites where sidewalk planting is not possible.

Special rules for four planned communities (Parkchester, Harlem River Houses, Fresh Meadows and Sunnyside Gardens) where demolition, construction or landscape alteration is not allowed as-of-right and needs City Planning Commission approval.
Review required for zoning changes and other discretionary actions to consider a project's potential environmental impacts and ways to address them.
A measure identified in environmental review to address a project's potential environmental impacts.

A zoning designation on a property for hazardous materials, noise or air quality so mitigation requirements are easy to find. The Office of Environmental Remediation (OER) must confirm required mitigations before DOB issues construction permits. Sites are listed in a Zoning Resolution appendix and on ZoLa.

An affordable housing program applying where rezonings allowed significant new housing. All new housing developments there must include a specified amount of permanently affordable housing, with an affordable housing plan worked out with HPD before DOB issues permits. MIH areas are mapped in ZR Appendix F.

Created in 2024, a program giving permanently affordable and supportive housing a higher FAR than other housing in all medium- and high-density districts that allow housing where MIH does not apply. Applicants work with HPD on an affordable housing plan. See ZR Section 12-10 and Article II, Chapter 7.
A defined term central to UAP that includes UAP developments. It is allowed a higher FAR (for example 3.9 instead of 3.0 in R6A) and higher maximum height than standard housing.

terms.term: Public Realm Improvement Fund Governing Group
terms.def: A group set up by zoning in East Midtown to administer a fund for public realm improvement projects; members include government agencies, elected officials, community boards and civic groups.

A council set up by zoning in the Theater District that uses a zoning-established fund to promote theater and theater-related uses. Members include City representatives, elected officials and theater industry representatives.

A single large zoning lot, or multiple lots planned as one project, for which applicants can seek CPC approval to alter zoning rules for a better site plan. There are residential, community facility and general types.
The City's online zoning and land use map. It shows zoning districts, special districts, (E) designations and rezonings, but is not the official zoning map; the "paper" pdf maps control.
DCP's website holding the official text of the Zoning Resolution, with search, clickable defined terms and cross references, section history buttons, and archived older versions.
Along the long dimension of a block, if the zoning map shows no boundary, the district boundary runs through the center of the block.

A C1 or C2 district mapped within a Residence District along neighborhood commercial corridors, shown as hatched areas on the zoning map. Each comes in five types (C1-1 to C1-5, C2-1 to C2-5) with different use and parking rules. All C2 hatches include dots.
A Special Purpose District with number suffixes (MX-4, MX-8, etc.) that pairs a Residence District with a Manufacturing District and sets how the two sets of rules work together.

The Zoning Resolution's levels of organization. Articles (Roman numerals) cover broad topics; each has up to nine chapters; chapters break into sections numbered by article and chapter, so Section 23-40 is Article II, Chapter 3, height and setback. Sections can divide into lettered paragraphs, numbered subparagraphs and romanettes.

Words given a specific meaning in the Zoning Resolution, shown in orange italics on the Online ZR. Core definitions are in Section 12-10; chapters may add their own. Common words can have special zoning meanings; "building" has a 200+ word definition.
A reference in zoning text to another section, used to point to applicable rules, identify which underlying rule is being modified, or reuse rules without repeating them.

Rules for reading zoning text: words take precedence over drawings or tables; "shall" is mandatory and "may" is permissive; "and" means all listed conditions apply, while "or" means one or more apply.

A ministerial action in which the City Planning Commission or its Chair confirms to DOB that a project meets specific conditions in the Zoning Resolution, like a checklist. Example: certification of a public plaza for a floor area bonus.
A discretionary CPC action allowing more limited modification of specific zoning rules, granted if the application meets conditions and findings in the Zoning Resolution.

A discretionary action allowing modification of specific zoning rules if the application meets listed findings. CPC special permits allow the broadest modifications and follow ULURP; BSA special permits allow limited modifications needing BSA's technical expertise.

Created in 2023, a defined term grouping renewable energy generation (such as solar panels) and energy storage (such as batteries) into a single use, allowed in all districts subject to size and screening rules. See ZR Section 12-10.

Created in 2021, a consistent level set 10 feet above grade from which owners in the highest-risk floodplain areas may measure height limits, to support resiliency improvements. Buildings using it must follow strict flood-resistant construction standards. See Article VI, Chapter 4.

Created in 2024, a framework of 15 new Manufacturing Districts ranging from 2 to 15 FAR that mimic older loft building forms and come in several use-mix options. First applied in the Atlantic Avenue Mixed Use area in Brooklyn. See Article IV.
The federal standard for classifying businesses. Since 2024, zoning uses NAICS to organize uses in Use Groups VI (Retail and Services) and X (Production).

Created in 2024, a defined term listing size and location conditions under which a lot in a lower-density district can use special use, bulk and parking rules to allow "missing middle" apartment buildings at the scale of older buildings. See ZR Section 12-10.

Residence Districts created in 2024 with the city's highest residential densities (15 and 18 FAR). They can only be mapped in Mandatory Inclusionary Housing areas; first applied in Midtown South. Contextual and Commercial District versions exist.

Created in 2024, a defined term for buildings meeting strict energy standards, which may take a five percent floor area deduction. Requirements differ for new and existing buildings. See ZR Section 12-10.
The Residence District whose residential bulk rules apply to housing in a given Commercial District, for example R6A for a C4-2A district.
DCP's service for zoning questions: call 212-720-3291 or submit an inquiry form on DCP's website; a zoning specialist responds within two business days.

rules.what: If a space with a non-conforming use stays vacant for more than two years, only conforming uses may occupy it. Small older shops in Residence Districts are exempt: new retail, service or office uses can re-occupy them at any time.
New apartment buildings with nine or more units must provide recreation space equal to three percent of residential floor area, indoors or outdoors, accessible to all residents.

New multi-family residential buildings must provide one enclosed bicycle parking space for every two dwelling units; commercial and community facility uses calculate requirements by size, and small establishments may waive out.

Zoning's typical required rear yard depth is 20 feet, applying in all districts for all building types, increased for narrow lots and upper parts of tall residential buildings, reduced for shallow lots, and not required on corner lots or full-block sites.
After damage or demolition, a non-complying building may be reconstructed if at least 25 percent of the building remains standing; more lenient rules apply to single- and two-family homes.

Most new buildings must provide street trees along the sidewalk; in low-density Residence Districts a planting strip along the curb is also required, and in Residence Districts planting is required between the building and the front property line. Parks can exempt sites where sidewalk planting is not possible.

On properties with an (E) designation, the Office of Environmental Remediation must confirm the project includes required hazardous materials, noise or air quality mitigations before DOB can issue construction permits.

Projects using MIH or UAP must work with HPD on an affordable housing plan before DOB issues construction permits, and HPD must sign off on finished units before DOB issues a certificate of occupancy.

rules.rule: Store size in neighborhood commercial districts
rules.what: Clothing and department stores cannot exceed 10,000 square feet in neighborhood commercial districts; the limit applies per business, not to the total on the lot.

rules.rule: Commercial uses in neighborhood commercial districts
rules.what: In neighborhood commercial districts, commercial uses are limited to the lower two stories of a building, with added access and nuisance controls where commercial and residential uses share the second story.

rules.rule: Sign size in C1 and C2 districts
rules.what: In C1 or C2 neighborhood commercial districts, a sign may equal three times the street frontage, up to a maximum of 150 square feet; each storefront calculates from its own frontage.
Most developments at the water's edge must provide public open space along it, meeting design and operational requirements; small lots, low-density residences and heavy manufacturing uses are exempt.
